Where is Orleans Parish and how is it laid out?

Orleans Parish is the Louisiana parish that covers the city of New Orleans, and the two share one set of boundaries. Since 1870 the parish and the city have been coextensive.

According to Wikipedia, the parish covers 349.85 square miles, but only 169.42 of those are land. The other 180.43 square miles are water, mostly from Lake Pontchartrain and Lake Borgne. The parish is bordered by St. Tammany Parish and Lake Pontchartrain to the north, St. Bernard Parish and Lake Borgne to the east, Plaquemines Parish to the south, and Jefferson Parish to the south and west.

The parish began as part of Orleans County in 1805 and was set apart as a civil parish in 1807. Jefferson Parish was carved out of its western and southern reaches in 1825. The 2020 census counted 383,997 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 362,184. For a seller, the practical point is that a single government handles zoning, code enforcement and tax billing, which keeps most of the paperwork in one place.

Who handles property tax in Orleans Parish?

Two offices do most of the work. The Orleans Parish Assessor values property and approves exemptions, and the City of New Orleans Bureau of the Treasury bills and collects the tax. The New Orleans City Council sits as the Board of Review for assessment appeals.

OfficeRoleContact from official pages
Orleans Parish AssessorValues property, approves homestead exemption, holds the tax roll1300 Perdido St, Room 4E01; (504) 754-8811; info@orleansassessors.com
Bureau of the TreasuryMails bills, collects payments, handles tax sales and refunds1300 Perdido St, Room 1W40; (504) 658-1712; taxresearchunit@nola.gov

The Treasury's own FAQ points sellers to the Assessor if a bill keeps arriving after the house has sold. You can read more on the Treasury FAQ page.

When are Orleans Parish property taxes due and what happens if they are late?

Orleans Parish bills are usually due January 31, and interest runs at 1 percent per month on the unpaid balance. The Treasury says bills normally go out in late December, though the date can shift depending on when the city sets the millage and when the bills are printed.

The 2026 bills carried a later deadline of February 28, 2026, according to the city's January 2026 announcement. That is different from most of Louisiana, where the state's property tax basics document says taxes are due December 31. If you are selling near the start of the year, check the bill itself instead of assuming a date.

A missed bill is not an excuse. The Treasury says that failing to receive a bill does not cancel interest, penalty or costs. If your bill did not arrive, you can look it up on the tax payment portal or call (504) 658-1712.

  • E-check payments online carry no service fee.
  • Card payments carry a third-party fee of about 2.49 percent.
  • Cash, checks and money orders are accepted for regular payments.
  • Partial payments can be made in person or by mail, but not online, and they do not stop interest or tax sale costs.

How is an Orleans Parish assessment calculated?

The Assessor sets fair market value, and the taxable amount is a percentage of that value. For Orleans Parish residential property, land and residential improvements are both assessed at 10 percent of market value. Commercial improvements are assessed at 15 percent.

The Council's appeals page gives a worked example. A $125,000 sale price becomes a $12,500 assessed value. After a $7,500 homestead exemption the taxable value is $5,000, and at a sample rate of 139.10 mills the tax comes to $695.50.

The Treasury lists 2026 city levies for police (4.67 mills) and fire (4.62 and 2.22 mills). We did not confirm a combined rate for any neighborhood, so check your own bill.

What does the Orleans Parish homestead exemption cover?

The homestead exemption removes the first $75,000 of market value, or $7,500 of assessed value, from most of the tax on a home you own and occupy.

Orleans differs from the rest of the state in one respect. The House Fiscal Division's property tax summary says the exemption applies to municipal property taxes in Orleans, while elsewhere it does not apply to municipal levies.

For sellers there are two practical effects:

  • The exemption belongs to you as the occupant. A buyer who plans to live in the house has to apply for his or her own.
  • If your bill has no homestead exemption, the city says payments go to recorded municipal liens, such as code enforcement liens, before they go to your taxes (City Code 6-39(d)). That rule does not apply to an occupied homestead property unless it holds a short-term rental permit or the lien comes from a Chapter 26 violation.

Homeowners aged 65 or older with qualifying income can also apply for the special assessment freeze. The Council page says the freeze ends on December 31 of the year the property is sold or the owner dies, so it does not pass to a buyer.

How do you appeal an Orleans Parish assessment?

Start with the Assessor during the public inspection period, then file a written appeal with the Board of Review if the dispute continues. The Council's calendar for the 2026 cycle lists the public inspection period as July 15 to August 17, 2026, with an appeal filing deadline of August 20, 2026.

Hearings run in September at Delgado Community College, City Park Campus, and written decisions follow in October. Dates change year to year, so confirm them on the Council appeals page.

The Board accepts three main kinds of evidence:

  • The recent sale price of the property.
  • Recent sale prices of comparable properties nearby.
  • The opinion of a real estate professional.

Appraisals, insurance policies, photographs and contractor repair estimates all help to support a claim of damage or over-valuation. The appeal form and all supporting papers must go in together, because an incomplete appeal is denied. If the Board's decision does not satisfy you, a written appeal to the Louisiana Tax Commission is due within 10 business days after notice of the decision. The Board cannot rule on homestead denials or age freeze decisions.

What is the Act 718 phase-in and does it affect a sale?

Act 718 of 2018 spreads out a large tax jump over four years for homeowners whose assessment rose more than 50 percent in a reassessment year. Qualifying parcels carry an "Act 718" marker on the tax bill.

The Treasury explains that Orleans was reassessed in two phases: 75 percent of the city for the 2020 tax year and the other 25 percent for 2021. Owners without a homestead exemption in the year of implementation do not qualify, and neither do commercial owners.

Buyers who purchase a property already under Act 718 do not qualify, so a new owner's first bill can be higher than yours. If an appeal lowers the assessment below the 50 percent threshold, the phase-in ends and a revised bill for the full amount comes due.

What happens if Orleans Parish taxes go unpaid and a tax sale follows?

The city changed its tax sale and adjudication process on January 1, 2026, and the Treasury says more details are coming. For tax sales held before that, the property owner has a redemption period, generally three years from the date the tax sale certificate is recorded. A valid blight judgment shortens that period to 18 months, and adjudications can run three to five years.

To redeem an older sale, the Treasury lists these payments:

  • The amount the tax sale purchaser paid at the sale.
  • Interest of 1 percent per month until redeemed.
  • A 5 percent penalty.
  • The current year's taxes and other debts.

Tax sale costs can also appear as a line on a bill. The Treasury says they cover the work of preparing a property for the upcoming sale. A tax sale claim or code lien will show up in a title search, and whoever closes the sale has to account for it.

How does a sale with property tax due work in Orleans Parish?

At closing, the title company or attorney finds the unpaid taxes and liens and pays them from the sale proceeds. Check the bill status, any municipal liens and the homestead exemption before the closing date.

Louisiana attaches a lien to each assessed property when the assessment roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages, under R.S. 47:1993. That lien generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances, apart from prior-year rolls and tax lien certificates. This is why unpaid taxes must be settled before a clean title passes.

Deeds are filed with the Clerk of Civil District Court in the Land Records Division, at 1340 Poydras Street, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Certified copies of recorded documents cost $30 each plus copy charges. Pages need a 2 inch top margin on the first sheet and 1 inch on the other sides, or the clerk can reject the document or add a $20 surcharge.

What is the property tax due date in Orleans Parish?

Orleans Parish bills are usually due January 31, and the 2026 bills were due February 28, 2026. Interest runs at 1 percent per month after the due date, and the city does not waive it for a bill that was never received.

Who do I call if I sold my house but still get the bill?

Call the Orleans Parish Assessor at (504) 754-8811. The Treasury says the Assessor handles ownership and mailing address changes, and that office can update the account.

What is the Orleans Parish homestead exemption?

It is $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, on a home you own and occupy. In Orleans it applies to municipal taxes as well, which is different from most of Louisiana.

Can I pay Orleans Parish property tax online?

Yes. The city accepts online e-check payments with no service fee and card payments with a fee of about 2.49 percent. Partial payments cannot be made online, so those must be mailed or paid in person at City Hall.

How long do I have to appeal to the Louisiana Tax Commission?

You have 10 business days after the Board of Review's notice is postmarked or delivered. The appeal must be in writing, and forms are linked from the City Council's appeals page.

What is Lafayette Parish, and which towns does it include?

Lafayette Parish is a small parish in Acadiana, covering 269 square miles of almost entirely dry land. Wikipedia ranks it the fifth smallest parish in Louisiana by land area.

Six municipalities sit inside it. Lafayette is the parish seat and largest city, and the others are Broussard (partly in St. Martin Parish), Carencro, Scott, Youngsville and the town of Duson (partly in Acadia Parish). Milton and Ossun are census-designated places with no city government of their own.

The distinction matters for tax, because a house in Youngsville, Scott or Carencro is billed differently from a house in the City of Lafayette or in unincorporated parish land. Before you read a bill, confirm which municipality, if any, taxes your address.

How does the Sheriff's tax department collect in Lafayette Parish?

The Lafayette Parish Sheriff's Office mails roughly 100,000 property tax notices every November. Its tax department states that the deadline to pay without penalty is December 31 each year.

The office does more than bill the parish. In 2004 it merged tax collection with Carencro and Youngsville, and in 2008 it added Scott and Duson. Their bills combine local and parish taxes into one payment, and the Sheriff disburses the funds to each government afterward. If you live in one of those five places, you can send a single check.

  • Payment methods: cash, personal check or credit card, and online through the Sheriff's Web Tax Site.
  • Hours: Monday to Thursday 7:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., Friday 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m.
  • Online fees: the Consolidated Government says e-check and card payments carry a transaction fee.

The City of Lafayette is the exception. It bills its own city tax, so a house inside the city may need two payments.

What does the Lafayette Parish Assessor actually do?

The Assessor finds and values property, and has very little say over how much tax you pay. The office describes its job as identifying, locating and fairly valuing all real and personal property in the parish. The taxing bodies, including the city-parish government, school board and sheriff, set the rates that turn that value into a bill.

State law requires reassessment at least every four years, although a value can change annually when sales move the market. The Assessor uses the sales comparison approach first, then cost and income approaches as checks, and keeps a GIS parcel map, ownership records and building descriptions. The site offers a tax estimator and a property search, and the office phone is (337) 291-7080.

Sellers can use the property search to see their own assessment before they talk to a buyer. A fair assessment and a fair price are different things, but a wide gap is worth asking about.

What relief programs does Lafayette Parish offer homeowners?

The homestead exemption is the most widely used break. It covers up to 160 acres with an owner-occupied residence and exempts $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, from state, parish and special taxes. It also applies to a pool, pool house or storage building belonging to the owner, but not to a second house or commercial building on the same land.

A separate assessed value freeze is available to qualifying owners. The Assessor says the freeze locks the assessed value at its January 1, 2025 level until the home is sold or remodeled, and it ends on the last day of December of the year before a sale. Eligibility requires a homestead exemption on the property and one of these:

  • Age 65 or older.
  • A permanent, total disability determined by a court, state or federal agency.
  • A service-connected veteran disability rating of 50% or more.

Adjusted gross income must be $100,000 or less. Taxes can still rise, because the millage rate can change even when the assessed value is frozen. Agricultural land can be assessed on use value if it is at least three acres or has produced at least $2,000 in gross income in each of the preceding four years.

How do you appeal a Lafayette Parish assessment?

Talk to a deputy assessor first, with evidence. To win a reduction you must show that the assessment is above market value and explain why. If you accept the deputy's answer, nothing more is required.

If you disagree, the Assessor's site says you may appeal to the Lafayette Consolidated Council during hearings held in September, with dates set by the Council in August. The Council reviews your material and the Assessor's information and rules at the hearing. A further appeal goes to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and Commission decisions are final unless appealed to district court within thirty days.

The current board's name and the exact filing cutoff were not confirmed on the pages we opened, because the city and parish councils were separated in 2018. Ask the Assessor for the filing date each summer.

What happens to unpaid taxes in Lafayette Parish?

Taxes unpaid after the December 31 deadline accrue interest, and a house can eventually be sold at the annual tax sale, held online on the first Wednesday in June. Under the Louisiana Constitution, property sold at tax sale can be redeemed for three years after recordation by paying the price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest.

Properties that nobody buys at the sale are called adjudicated. Lafayette Consolidated Government's disposition process lets someone apply for one only after three consecutive years of adjudication. A public bid starts at a minimum of 75% of the Assessor's fair market value, and a second round, about a month later, starts at 33%. Outstanding taxes and liens are waived when the correct affidavit is recorded, and applicants are urged to hire an attorney with title experience.

The owner can redeem at any time until the act of sale to the applicant is recorded, by paying all taxes, liens and fees to both the city and the Sheriff. For a seller, that is the clearest reason to resolve arrears before they turn into an adjudication.

How does a sale with taxes owed work in Lafayette Parish?

Taxes owed are settled from the proceeds when the house sells. A closing agent can request a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901, which shows whether state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes are paid, except those for the year of the sale.

A cash sale avoids the delay that comes with a buyer's mortgage and appraisal. Tax bills, inherited homes, tenants and repairs are the situations where speed helps. After closing, the buyer files a new homestead claim and the Assessor updates ownership, which the office tracks as part of its parcel work.

The act itself must be recorded with the Lafayette Parish Clerk of Court. See our clerk of court guide for fees and steps.

Who collects property tax in Lafayette Parish?

The Lafayette Parish Sheriff's Office tax department mails about 100,000 notices each November and collects payments. The City of Lafayette bills its own city tax separately.

What is the Lafayette Parish tax deadline?

The Sheriff's deadline for paying without penalty is December 31 each year. Unpaid amounts then accrue interest and can lead to the tax sale in June.

What is the Lafayette Parish homestead exemption?

It exempts $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of market value, for an owner-occupied home on up to 160 acres. The owner claims it with the Assessor.

Can seniors freeze their Lafayette Parish assessment?

Owners 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability, can apply for an assessed value freeze if they hold a homestead exemption and have adjusted gross income of $100,000 or less. The freeze fixes the January 1, 2025 value.

Can I sell my Lafayette Parish house with back taxes?

Yes. The taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Selling before adjudication keeps you in control of the property and stops interest from growing.

What is Caddo Parish and how is it laid out?

Caddo Parish is in the northwest corner of Louisiana, with Shreveport as its parish seat and largest city. Wikipedia's parish entry reports a 2020 population of 237,848 and a total area of 937 square miles, about 58 of them water. Shreveport grew along the Red River and is the center of the Ark-La-Tex region.

The legislature created the parish in 1838 from Natchitoches Parish and named it for the Caddo people. Bossier Parish lies directly east, across the river, with Arkansas to the north and Texas to the west and southwest. The parish holds eleven incorporated places, which gives owners several different local governments to deal with.

TypePlaces in Caddo Parish
CityShreveport
TownsBlanchard, Greenwood, Mooringsport, Oil City, Vivian
VillagesBelcher, Gilliam, Hosston, Ida, Rodessa

Interstates 20, 220 and 49 cross the parish, along with U.S. 71, 79, 80 and 171.

What does the Caddo Parish economy look like for homeowners?

Most of the parish economy runs through Shreveport, and the numbers show uneven incomes. Wikipedia names Amazon and Walmart among the large employers and lists LSU Health Sciences Center in Shreveport. It also reports that about 22.9% of residents lived at or below the poverty line in 2020, and that parishwide median household income was $42,003 in the 2020 American Community Survey.

Those figures matter to sellers because an owner on a tight income can fall behind on a bill that arrives once a year, and the parish runs an annual tax lien auction for unpaid balances.

The Caddo Parish School Board runs the public schools across the whole parish.

Who handles Caddo Parish property tax?

The Caddo Parish Assessor values every parcel and the Caddo Parish Sheriff collects the parish tax. The Sheriff's FAQ states plainly that the Sheriff does not decide how much you owe, and that the Assessor's Office, in Room 102 of the courthouse, is separate from the Sheriff.

  • Assessor: Caddo Parish Courthouse, Room 102, (318) 226-6701 for address changes and value questions.
  • Sheriff's Tax Department: Caddo Parish Courthouse, 1st Floor, 501 Texas Street, Room 101, Shreveport, open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM; phone (318) 681-0638 for balances.
  • Mail payments to the Property Tax Dept., P.O. Box 20905, Shreveport, LA 71120-0905.
  • Shreveport city tax is collected separately by the city, at (318) 673-5500, and does not appear on the Sheriff's notice.

Outside Shreveport, nine parish fire districts provide fire protection, and their fees are set by voters in each district. Shreveport residents fund fire service through city taxes instead.

How does the Caddo assessor set a value?

Caddo uses three approaches: comparing recent sales, estimating replacement cost less depreciation, and looking at the income a property could earn. The Assessor's FAQ also warns that a sale made under pressure, such as an owner who needed cash fast, can distort a comparison, so the office studies many sales.

Louisiana then applies a fixed percentage to the market value to reach the assessed value.

ClassShare of market value assessed
Land10%
Residential improvements, including apartments10%
Commercial improvements15%
Business movable property15%
Public service, excluding land25%

Millage then converts the assessed value to tax. The Sheriff's example at 150 mills puts tax at $1,500 on $10,000 of assessed value, or $375 after a $7,500 homestead exemption. That illustration uses a round rate, so read your own notice for the real one.

Who qualifies for exemptions and freezes in Caddo Parish?

An owner who lives in the home qualifies for the homestead exemption, which removes parish tax on the first $75,000 of market value. It applies to one home, not to city taxes, and not to fire district fees. File as soon as you become the owner; the exemption stays until the owner changes or the home stops being the primary residence.

  • Disabled veterans: a 100% service-connected rating, confirmed by a Veterans Administration form, can qualify for up to $75,000 of additional homestead.
  • Age 65 and older: a special assessment level freezes the assessed value if adjusted gross income was under $100,000. It is lost if the property is transferred or improvements exceed 25% of its value, and a surviving spouse over 55 can qualify.
  • Disabled owners under 65: a freeze is available with 100% Social Security disability or a 50% service-connected rating, but it must be reapplied for each year.

The office requires proof of the previous year's income, such as a tax return or a Social Security statement.

What are the 2026 Caddo assessment and appeal dates?

For 2026 the Caddo assessor opened the books on August 17 and closed public inspection on August 31. According to the office's news page, all appeals had to be received by 5:00 p.m. on September 8, and the Board of Review heard appeals on September 14 at 1:00 p.m. at the Caddo Commission.

The Assessor's FAQ explains why timing matters: the open-roll period is when an owner can legally file a protest. Many taxpayers wait for the bill that arrives around the first of December, and the office will discuss the assessment then, but a protest can no longer be filed at that point. If you missed this year's window, mark the late-August dates in next year's calendar.

When is Caddo Parish property tax due and what happens when it is late?

Caddo taxes must be paid by December 31, and the Sheriff's FAQ says notices are generally mailed in the last week of November. After December 31 the tax is delinquent, with interest of 1% per month. Taxes not fully paid by January 31 add a 10% collection fee, and unpaid accounts after that date add the cost of notices and newspaper advertising.

Payments post to the account number you give, and a payment to the wrong account is final. Partial payments are allowed, but the unpaid balance keeps growing and the parcel is still offered at the annual auction.

What happens to a Caddo house at a tax lien auction?

The Sheriff sells a tax lien certificate at an online auction, and the winning bidder is the person who will take the least ownership interest in the property while paying the full unpaid taxes. That description appears in the Caddo Sheriff's FAQ, and it matches the new statewide lien approach that the Bossier Sheriff describes as effective January 1, 2026. A property that draws no bid is transferred to the parish, which can sometimes sell it to a third party.

The Assessor's FAQ adds that adjudicated property can be found through the CPTA Professional Search subscription or by visiting the courthouse, and that phone requests are not answered. Because the rules changed in 2026, a Caddo owner with a delinquent balance should ask the Sheriff what the lien process allows today.

How does Caddo property tax work when you sell?

The Sheriff does not split the bill between buyer and seller, so the full year's tax stays on the property until someone pays it. A buyer who closes after January 1 may find the account still in the prior owner's name, and the Sheriff's FAQ says the new owner is responsible for checking what is owed.

  • Get the current balance from the Sheriff's Tax Department before choosing a closing date.
  • Check city tax with Shreveport separately, since it is billed apart from the parish.
  • Ask your mortgage servicer for proof of payment if escrow covers the tax, because the Sheriff posts the first payment it receives and will not reverse a duplicate.
  • Have the new owner file for homestead soon after closing.

Where is Jefferson Parish and how is it laid out?

Jefferson Parish sits in southeast Louisiana on both banks of the Mississippi River, next to New Orleans. The Census Bureau counts 665 square miles in total, but only 296 of them are land because 56% of the area is water.

Lake Pontchartrain forms the northern edge, and the river runs through roughly the middle. Orleans Parish lies downriver to the east, St. Charles Parish upriver to the west, and Plaquemines Parish to the southeast. Most of the southern half of the parish is uninhabited marsh, with Grand Isle as one of the exceptions.

The parish seat is Gretna, the largest community is Metairie, and the largest incorporated city is Kenner. Other incorporated places are Harahan, Westwego, Grand Isle and Jean Lafitte. Harvey, Marrero, Terrytown and Old Metairie are unincorporated or sit inside larger municipalities, so the office that bills your property tax is the same whichever name is on your mailing address.

Residents describe the parish in two halves. East Jefferson is the Metairie, Kenner and Harahan side, and West Jefferson (the Westbank) covers Gretna, Harvey, Marrero and Westwego.

How did Jefferson Parish grow into the neighborhoods sellers see today?

The Louisiana Legislature created Jefferson Parish on February 11, 1825. The present line with Orleans Parish was fixed in 1874, and the seat moved to Gretna that same year.

Most of today's housing stock came after World War II. The parish population doubled from 1940 to 1950 and again from 1950 to 1960, as families moved from New Orleans into new subdivisions of detached houses. East Jefferson filled in along Jefferson Highway and Airline Highway, then along Veterans Boulevard, and Interstate 10 arrived in the early 1960s.

On the Westbank, large-scale building began after the Greater New Orleans Bridge opened in 1958. Terrytown inside Gretna was the first big subdivision, followed by Harvey, Marrero, Westwego and Avondale.

The sheriff's website explains that the Sheriff also serves as ex-officio tax collector, under the Louisiana Constitution, state statutes and the parish code of ordinances. Under the statewide rules summarized by the Louisiana House Fiscal Division, tax equals the millage rate multiplied by the assessed value. Residential property is assessed at 10% of fair market value, and millage is set by local ordinance after voter approval. A home inside a municipality such as Kenner or Gretna pays several levies at once: the parish, the school board, the city and possibly special districts.

The sheriff also tells owners that the assessor must send any change in an assessment to the Louisiana Tax Commission for approval, so the Commission is the last administrative stop for value disputes.

When are Jefferson Parish property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?

Jefferson Parish bills become due when the notice arrives and are delinquent after December 31. The sheriff's overview for the 2025 bills gives December 31, 2025 as the delinquency date and describes a short grace window for payments made or postmarked just after it, which the parish listing puts at January 2, 2026. Read the date printed on your own notice, because it can shift with the calendar.

Once a bill is late, the sheriff's FAQ states that interest runs at 1% per month from January 1 until paid. The sheriff accepts a postmark as proof of timely mailing, but the office points out that you are responsible for making sure the Post Office actually postmarks the envelope in time.

  • Partial payments are taken, but interest and other costs keep running. The costs the sheriff lists include certified mail, advertisements and mortgage certificate fees.

  • The sheriff says it does not sell property for non-payment, yet it does run tax sales or auctions that can, after several years, move ownership.
  • Statewide, the constitution gives a tax debtor three years after recordation of a tax sale to redeem the property by paying the price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest, according to an Attorney General opinion.

How do you challenge a Jefferson Parish assessment?

Start with the Assessor during the open-rolls period, because the form itself warns that no assessment changes can be made after the inspection period ends. The Jefferson Parish Assessor's appeal form says the rolls are open for fifteen calendar days, beginning no earlier than August 1 and ending no later than September 15, as set by R.S. 47:1992.1.

The form is strict. All requested information must be submitted, and an incomplete form is denied. You need enough documentation to show the assessment may be wrong, and the office says there is no guarantee it will agree to a change.

  • Photos must show the whole structure as seen from the street, and interior damage photos must show the entire room. Photocopied photos are refused.
  • Repair estimates, an appraisal or a letter of explanation can be attached.
  • If you are not the owner, a Tax Authorization Form must accompany the request.
  • Each property needs its own form. The apartment version also asks for income and expense statements for the two prior calendar years and occupancy rates.

If the Assessor does not move, the next step is the parish Board of Review, and a ruling there can be appealed to the Louisiana Tax Commission. The exact filing deadline for the Board of Review was not shown on the pages we opened, so ask the Assessor for the current calendar each summer.

What does the Jefferson Parish homestead exemption require?

You must sign for the homestead exemption in person at one of the two Assessor offices. Bring a copy of your act of sale and a photo ID showing the address of the home. When a husband and wife own jointly, only one has to appear.

The state constitution exempts the first $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of fair market value, from state, parish and special taxes. After you file, a receipt arrives in the mail each year showing the exemption is permanent. The assessor's site also carries separate applications for first responders and volunteer firefighters, with a September 1 filing cutoff for the current tax year.

For sellers, the exemption ends with the sale. A buyer who plans to live in the house files a new claim after the act of sale, which is why a deed copy is the first document the Assessor asks for.

What does storm and flood history mean for a Jefferson Parish house?

Hurricane Katrina is the reference point most buyers and insurers use. When it made landfall on August 29, 2005, the East Bank saw widespread flooding and wind damage, while the West Bank had little to no flooding but plenty of wind damage. Jefferson's levees and floodwalls did not fail, which let floodwater be pumped out quickly.

The parish Department of Floodplain Management and Hazard Mitigation (504-736-6540) can tell you whether a lot sits in a regulated flood zone. If damage from a storm has lowered a home's condition, document it, because the assessor's appeal form asks for repair estimates and photos, and a damaged house can support a lower valuation during the inspection window.

How does a sale with property tax due work in Jefferson Parish?

Taxes owed on the house are paid from the sale proceeds at closing, so an unpaid bill does not block a sale. Louisiana law lets any party to an act of sale for property outside New Orleans obtain a certificate showing whether state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes are paid, except for the year of the sale (R.S. 9:2901).

The transfer then has to be recorded. Civil Code article 3338 says an instrument that transfers an immovable has no effect against third persons until it is recorded in the conveyance records, so the closing attorney or title company files the act with the clerk.

Sellers with back taxes, a storm-damaged roof or a tenant in place often prefer a buyer who closes as-is. The sheriff also publishes a real estate sales list for judicial sales, which is worth checking if a lender or a creditor has already moved against the property.

The Jefferson Parish Sheriff collects it as ex-officio tax collector. The Assessor, with offices in Gretna and Harahan, sets the value, and the Louisiana Tax Commission approves assessment changes.

What is the interest on late Jefferson Parish property tax?

The sheriff's FAQ lists interest at 1% per month from January 1 until the bill is paid. Partial payments are accepted but interest and costs such as certified mail and advertising continue to build.

When can I dispute my Jefferson Parish assessment?

Only during the open-rolls period, which the Assessor's form describes as fifteen calendar days beginning no earlier than August 1 and ending no later than September 15. After it closes, no assessment changes can be made.

Can I sell my Jefferson Parish house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The taxes are paid from the proceeds at closing, and a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901 shows what is outstanding. A cash buyer who closes as-is can still complete the purchase.

Where do I file for a homestead exemption in Jefferson Parish?

In person at either Assessor office, at 200 Derbigny St. in Gretna or 1221 Elmwood Park Blvd. in Harahan. Bring your act of sale and a photo ID showing the home address.

Houma is the parish seat and largest city, and Wikipedia says it was settled by the Chitimacha and then the Houma people before European colonization. Founding dates for the city differ between 1832 and 1834, and incorporation came in 1848.

Wikipedia lists Bayou Cane, Montegut, Dulac, Chauvin, Dularge, Gibson and Pointe-au-Chien among the parish's communities. The Houma metro area, which also includes the Thibodaux area, had 208,178 people in 2020.

Houma-Terrebonne Airport is about 3 miles southeast of the downtown area, and Good Earth Transit runs five major bus routes, including service to Thibodaux. Most residents rely on cars. The Intracoastal Waterway and the Houma Navigational Canal remain part of local commerce.

Vietnamese refugee families settled in the area in the 1970s, and many still work in shrimping, which is one of several ways the fishing economy shows up in local property types, from bayou camps to older homes near docks.

Where is Ouachita Parish and what towns does it include?

Ouachita Parish sits in northern Louisiana, and its parish seat is Monroe, which is also its largest municipality. West Monroe lies across the Ouachita River from Monroe, and the two cities are the parish's only incorporated cities. The towns are Richwood and Sterlington.

Wikipedia gives the parish a total area of 632 square miles, with 610 of them land. The 2020 census counted 160,368 people, and the 2025 estimate is 158,542. Interstate 20, U.S. 80 and U.S. 165 cross the parish.

Neighbors are Union Parish to the north, Morehouse to the northeast, Richland to the east, Caldwell to the south, Jackson to the southwest and Lincoln to the west. Unincorporated communities that appear on property records include Bawcomville, Brownsville, Calhoun, Claiborne, Lakeshore and Swartz.

What shaped the Ouachita Parish housing stock?

Housing in the parish reflects several waves of growth. Wikipedia reports that the Monroe natural gas field was discovered in 1916 and covered more than 500 square miles. For a time Monroe was known as the natural gas capital of the world.

The population of the parish rose by more than 79 percent between 1920 and 1930, to roughly 54,000 people, as workers arrived. The census figures in the same article show the parish passing 100,000 residents in 1960 and reaching 160,368 in 2020.

A railroad bridge over the river opened in 1883, and Sterlington and Richwood were incorporated in 1961 and 1974. A seller with a house from any of these building waves should expect the age of the roof, wiring and plumbing to shape what a buyer asks for.

Who works in Ouachita Parish and what does it mean for sellers?

Wikipedia, citing the North Louisiana Economic Partnership, lists a mix of technology, health care, government, finance and manufacturing employers at the top of the parish.

The University of Louisiana at Monroe is also in Monroe. Public schools outside Monroe are run by the Ouachita Parish School Board, and the Monroe City School System serves areas within Monroe. Which district a house falls in depends on its address, so check before you describe schools to a buyer.

Who handles property tax in Ouachita Parish?

The Ouachita Parish Assessor values property, and the Ouachita Parish Sheriff collects the tax. The Louisiana Constitution and Legislature set the framework, and the Louisiana Tax Commission writes the assessment rules. Local bodies such as the police jury and school board set the levies that appear on a bill.

OfficeWhat it doesOfficial detail
Ouachita Parish AssessorLists and values all taxable property, tracks homestead exemptionsAssessor Stephanie Smith; records searchable online

The Assessor's website at opassessor.com carries a property search, an interactive map, millage rates by ward and a tax calculator. The Sheriff's office posts tax information at opso.net.

How is a Ouachita Parish assessment worked out?

The Assessor takes fair market value and multiplies it by a statutory percentage. According to the Assessor's FAQ, land is assessed at 10 percent of fair market value and residential improvements at 10 percent. Commercial property, including personal property, is at 15 percent, though commercial land is at 10 percent.

The office gives a worked example. A $100,000 home is assessed at $10,000. After the $7,500 maximum homestead exemption, the taxable value is $2,500, and at 120 mills the parish taxes are $300. The office adds that the homestead exemption does not reduce city taxes, so a house inside Monroe or West Monroe can see a higher total than a house outside them.

Louisiana requires reassessment at least every four years, and a property can be reassessed at any time after a sale or a change. The Assessor also asks new buyers to complete a Sales Questionnaire, which helps check fair market value.

When are Ouachita Parish property taxes due?

Under Louisiana's general rule, bills go out in December and taxes are due December 31, with interest of 1 percent per month on late balances. The House Fiscal Division's property tax summary states those terms for parishes statewide.

The Sheriff's office is the collector, and the Tax Office takes payments by mail, in person or online. We could not open a current notice with the exact deadline posted by the Sheriff, so treat December 31 as the general rule and check your bill and the Sheriff's website for the year in question.

The Assessor's FAQ warns that a missing notice does not excuse payment. If you did not receive a bill, you can ask the tax collector what is owed.

  • Bills are mailed once a year, in December.
  • Late balances accrue interest at 1 percent a month.
  • Unpaid property can go to a tax sale, and a debtor has three years to redeem immovable property sold that way.
  • Foreclosure and seizure sales run through the Sheriff's Civil Division, with auctions on Wednesday mornings at 10 a.m. through an online platform.

How do you challenge a Ouachita Parish assessment?

Talk to the Assessor first, then appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review if the disagreement stays. After that, an appeal can go to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and finally to the courts.

The Assessor's office asks owners to bring evidence that its valuation is wrong. Recent sale prices, an appraisal and photographs of damage are the kinds of material that other Louisiana boards accept. Louisiana law lets the public inspect the tax roll in a window between August 15 and September 15 outside Orleans Parish.

We did not find a published Board of Review deadline for Ouachita Parish, so call the Assessor before the inspection period ends. Missing the appeal window usually means waiting for the next tax year.

What exemptions can lower a Ouachita Parish tax bill?

The main reductions are the homestead exemption and the special assessment freeze for older owners. The homestead exemption is $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, for an owner-occupied home. It can cover up to 160 acres that include an owner-occupied residence.

The Assessor's website links to an application postcard and a page about the 65 and older Special Assessment Value Freeze. State guidance says the freeze can also apply to owners with a service-connected disability of at least 50 percent, subject to an income limit. The Assessor also publishes a veterans brochure. A buyer needs to apply on his or her own, since both benefits are tied to the person living in the home.

What should you know about selling a Ouachita Parish house with tax due?

Unpaid taxes are a lien on the property and must be cleared for a clean title to pass. Under La. R.S. 47:1993, once the assessment roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages, it acts as a lien and privilege on each assessed property, and it generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances.

In practice the closing attorney or title company asks the Sheriff's Tax Office for a payoff and pays it from the proceeds. Deeds are recorded with the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court, whose office is on South Grand Street in Monroe. If the house also carries a mortgage, back taxes and repairs, the title work can take longer, so start the payoff request early.

Check the Assessor's property search for your parcel's current owner and homestead status before you list. Errors found there are easier to fix before a buyer's attorney finds them.

When are Ouachita Parish property taxes due?

The general Louisiana rule is December 31, and late balances accrue 1 percent interest per month. Confirm the exact year's deadline with the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Tax Office at (318) 324-2536.

Who collects property tax in Ouachita Parish?

The Ouachita Parish Sheriff, acting as ex-officio tax collector. Payments can be made by mail, in person or online through the Sheriff's website.

What is the Ouachita Parish homestead exemption?

It is $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of fair market value, on an owner-occupied home. The Assessor's FAQ says it does not apply to city taxes.

How do I appeal my Ouachita Parish assessment?

Meet with the Assessor, then appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review, then to the Louisiana Tax Commission. We could not confirm a Board of Review deadline, so ask the Assessor.

What happens if I do not pay?

Interest accrues at 1 percent a month, and the property can be sold at a tax sale. A debtor has three years to redeem immovable property sold that way.

Do I owe property tax at closing in Ouachita Parish?

Unpaid taxes are a lien and have to be cleared for clear title, so the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds. Your closing attorney or title company will request the figure from the Tax Office.
